signal.title: [Bug]: GET /health returns extra_headers and aws_session_token in plaintext
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. Related, not a duplicate: #18818 fixed masking of `extra_headers` on `/model/info`. `GET /health` is a different sanitizer. It still returns those values in full. `api_key` is stripped (CVE-2025-11203 class). `extra_headers` and `aws_session_token` were never added to that strip list. ### What happened? LiteLLM 1.96.2. No master key. A deployment in `config.yaml` has `extra_headers` (Azure `api-key`, Google `x-goog-api-key`, a Bearer token) and `aws_session_token`. `GET /health` returns those values in plaintext on the healthy (or unhealthy) row. `api_key` is absent. `api_base` is absent for a non-admin caller. The extra headers stay. This was reproduced with fake `CANARY_*` strings, not real provider keys. A live proxy with a normal `api_key: os.environ/...` and no `extra_headers` does not echo the resolved key on `/model/info` (`api_key` is popped). The hole is specifically fields that are not `api_key`. Expected: `/health` should omit or mask `extra_headers`, `headers`, and `aws_session_token` the same way it already omits `api_key`. ### User Flow Before a (hypothetical) fix: a tenant who can call `/health` can read the admin's upstream credentials out of the JSON. 1. The proxy admin puts provider auth in `litellm_params.extra_headers` (and optionally `aws_session_token`) in `config.yaml`, then starts the proxy on `http://127.0.0.1:4000`. 2. Any caller sends `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/health` with no `Authorization` header (default install, no master key). 3. HTTP 200. The `healthy_endpoints` (or `unhealthy_endpoints`) row contains `extra_headers.Authorization`, `extra_headers.x-goog-api-key`, `extra_headers.api-key`, and `aws_session_token` in full. 4. That caller can take those values and call the provider directly, bypassing the proxy. After a (hypothetical) fix: the same `/health` call still reports healthy/unhealthy, but those secret fields are gone or masked. 1. The proxy admin uses the same `config.yaml` and starts the same proxy. 2. The same caller sends `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/health`. 3. HTTP 200. The row still has `model` and health status. It does not contain the `extra_headers` values or `aws_session_token`. 4. That caller cannot recover the admin's upstream credentials from `/health`. ### Proof the bug occurs Config / setup the proxy ran with: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: mock litellm_params: model: openai/mockmodel api_base: http://127.0.0.1:9996/v1 api_key: sk-x-CANARY_DEPLOYMENT_API_KEY extra_headers: Authorization: Bearer CANARY_EXTRA_HEADERS_AUTHORIZATION x-goog-api-key: CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE api-key: CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY aws_session_token: CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE ``` The backend at `127.0.0.1:9996` is a local OpenAI-compatible stub that returns HTTP 200 so the row lands in `healthy_endpoints`. The leak is the proxy copying `litellm_params` into the `/health` body. It does not depend on a real provider key. You can drop the stub: point `api_base` at `http://127.0.0.1:1`. The health check fails, and the same fields still appear under `unhealthy_endpoints`. No API key required. Version or commit: LiteLLM **1.96.2** Commands and their full output: ``` curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4000/health ``` ```json { "healthy_endpoints": [ { "model": "openai/mockmodel", "extra_headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer CANARY_EXTRA_HEADERS_AUTHORIZATION", "x-goog-api-key": "CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE", "api-key": "CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY" }, "aws_session_token": "CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE" } ], "unhealthy_endpoints": [], "healthy_count": 1, "unhealthy_count": 0 } ``` `api_key` is not in that object. `GET /v1/models` and `GET /health/liveliness` do not contain the canaries. Copy-paste repro, no keys, no stub: ```yaml # leak.yaml model_list: - model_name: demo litellm_params: model: openai/gpt-4o-mini api_base: http://127.0.0.1:1 api_key: sk-not-a-real-key extra_headers: x-goog-api-key: CANARY_X_GOOG_API_KEY_VALUE api-key: CANARY_AZURE_STYLE_API_KEY aws_session_token: CANARY_AWS_SESSION_TOKEN_VALUE ``` ``` litellm --config leak.yaml --port 4000 --host 127.0.0.1 curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4000/health ``` The canaries show up on the unhealthy row. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.96.2

signal.title: feat(proxy): add config source precedence toggle
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Saved proxy settings can override newer deployment values - Operators cannot explicitly choose configuration precedence How it solves it: - Adds database or config file precedence selection - Limits precedence changes to LiteLLM_Config-backed settings - Keeps nonconflicting values from the lower-priority source ## User Flow Before: a proxy admin deploys a setting change, but an older saved value remains active 1. They POST a proxy setting to `https://litellm-domain/config/update`, receiving HTTP 200 2. They change the same setting in their deployment config and roll out the proxy 3. The proxy continues using the saved value instead of the newly deployed value 4. They must clear the saved setting before the deployment change takes effect After: the same deployment can explicitly make its config values authoritative 1. They POST a proxy setting to `https://litellm-domain/config/update`, receiving HTTP 200 2. They set `general_settings.config_source_of_truth: config_file`, change the same setting, and roll out the proxy 3. The proxy uses the explicit deployed value while retaining saved settings that do not conflict 4. Restarts and periodic reloads continue applying the selected precedence ## Relevant issues Resolves #36564 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Pending a database-backed live proxy run ## Type New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - Existing installations retain database precedence until explicitly changed - LLM model storage and other database tables retain existing behavior ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: test(ui): await the playground model combobox before clicking it
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - A playground test fails at random in full-suite runs - Its model-picker lookup does not wait for loading - Retrying hid the flake instead of fixing it How it solves it: - The shared helper now awaits the model picker - The lookup retries until loading finishes ## User Flow This PR changes no runtime behavior, so there is no end-user flow to walk. The people who hit it are the ones running the dashboard unit suite, so the two lists below are written from that seat Before: a contributor running the dashboard suite gets a red playground test they cannot reproduce 1. They run `npx vitest run` in `ui/litellm-dashboard` 2. The run reports `ChatUI > should show Simulate failure to test fallbacks in Model Settings when chat endpoint is selected` as failed, with `TestingLibraryElementError: Unable to find an element with the placeholder text of: Select a Model` 3. They re-run that one file and it passes every time, so the failure looks unreal 4. They re-run the whole suite and it comes back fully green, 646 files and 7019 tests 5. Nothing in the diff explains either result, so the run gets retried rather than fixed, and a genuine failure in that test would be waved through the same way After: the same suite run is stable, so red means a real defect 1. They run `npx vitest run` in `ui/litellm-dashboard` 2. The playground test waits for the model picker to finish loading before it clicks it 3. The suite reports 646 files and 7019 tests passing, run after run 4. A failure in that test now points at behavior that actually broke ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist **Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR** - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [ ] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [ ] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review (Greptile reviews automatically once the PR is opened; only comment `@greptileai` to re-request a review after pushing changes) ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix This PR touches one line of one vitest file and no shipped code, so there is nothing to curl and no live-proxy behavior to capture. The proof is a deterministic red/green of the race instead The model picker renders its own placeholder from the loading flag, so the text the helper searched for does not exist while models are loading: ```tsx placeholder={isLoadingModels ? "Loading models..." : "Select a Model"} disabled={isLoadingModels} ``` `isLoadingModels` starts `false`, but `render()` flushes the mount effect and the flag flips to `true` before the first `await` in the loader. The control the helper wants is therefore already gone when the test body starts, and only returns once the mocked fetch resolves. The `waitFor` for the page heading that precedes every call passes on its first tick, since that heading renders unconditionally, so it gates nothing To make the window deterministic, I copied the failing test and changed only the mocked fetch, from resolving on a microtask to resolving on a macrotask, then flipped the helper line back and forth with everything else held identical Before, at `e0f388cb5c`, with `screen.getByPlaceholderText`: ``` × ChatUI flake repro > should show Simulate failure to test fallbacks in Model Settings when chat endpoint is selected 85ms → Unable to find an element with the placeholder text of: Select a Model TestingLibraryElementError: Unable to find an element with the placeholder text of: Select a Model Test Files 1 failed (1) Tests 1 failed (1) ``` After, at `f861af42c0`, with `await screen.findByPlaceholderText`: ``` ✓ src/app/(dashboard)/playground/components/chat_ui/ChatUIFlakeRepro.test.tsx (1 test) 275ms Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 1 passed (1) ``` That reproduces the exact error text on the exact test that failed in the wild. The scratch copy was deleted afterwards and is not part of this diff Single-file runs never showed the flake, so the check that counts is the whole dashboard suite. Two consecutive full runs at `f861af42c0`, both clean: ``` $ cd ui/litellm-dashboard && npx vitest run Test Files 646 passed (646) Tests 7019 passed (7019) Duration 255.87s ``` Those two runs predate the merge of `litellm_internal_staging` into this branch, which brought in dashboard changes of its own. On the merged tree I re-ran the playground file alone, 18 tests passing, and left the full-suite re-run to CI ## Type ✅ Test ## Caveats (if any) - Test-only change, no shipped code touched - Audited the file's other lookups, no second race ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: feat(proxy): add a live registry of active requests
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: There is no way to see what a proxy is serving right now, or for whom. A request that has not finished yet is in no spend log, traces show its spans without telling you who issued it, and `litellm_in_flight_requests` is a count with no identity attached. When one caller saturates a model you cannot answer "whose traffic is this" without waiting for the requests to finish. How it solves it: A Redis-backed registry records every authenticated request at pre-call time and removes it when the HTTP response finishes, so `GET /global/active_requests` can answer that question across replicas, and the admin UI gets a page that lists, sorts and filters the live set, opens any request's full detail, and cancels one that is stuck https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/40cebc2f-c6ae-4a42-ae1c-7be88503fa1c ## Relevant issues ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Delays in PR merge? If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA). ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Ran against a live proxy on `localhost:4000` in front of a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint, so these are real generations on real hardware rather than mocks. Six concurrent streaming completions were fired across two models, each asked for a 1500 word answer so they stay in flight long enough to read the endpoint: ```bash for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do m=$([ $((i%2)) -eq 0 ] && echo Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512 || echo gpt-oss-120b) curl -s -o /dev/null -N http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"model\":\"$m\",\"stream\":true,\"max_tokens\":2000,\"user\":\"end-user-$i\", \"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Write a detailed 1500 word explanation of how a Redis sorted set works internally.\"}]}" & done ``` While they run: ```bash $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ "http://localhost:4000/global/active_requests?page_size=3" | jq { "available": true, "reason": null, "items": [ { "request_id": "b545affc-f1ae-4f54-9866-1eb424937000", "started_at": 1786002556.584499, "model": "Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512", "call_type": "acompletion", "streaming": true, "route": "/v1/chat/completions", "user_id": "default_user_id", "user_email": null, "end_user_id": "end-user-6", "organization_id": null, "organization_alias": null, "project_id": null, "project_alias": null, "team_id": null, "team_alias": null, "key_alias": null, "key_hash_prefix": "litellm_prox", "pod": null } ], "total": 6, "page": 1, "page_size": 3, "truncated": false, "generated_at": "2026-08-06T07:49:16.584Z" } ``` `end_user_id` comes straight from the OpenAI standard `user` field on the request, so filtering by caller works without any extra configuration: ```bash $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ "http://localhost:4000/global/active_requests?end_user_id=end-user-3" \ | jq '{total, models: [.items[].model], end_users: [.items[].end_user_id]}' { "total": 1, "models": ["gpt-oss-120b"], "end_users": ["end-user-3"] } ``` After the six generations finished, the registry is empty again and so is the Redis index, which is the cleanup path running in the response `finally`: ```bash $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ "http://localhost:4000/global/active_requests" | jq '.total' 0 $ redis-cli zcard "litellm:active_requests:index" (integer) 0 ``` Cancelling a request that was mid-generation on a real model: ```bash $ curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ "http://localhost:4000/global/active_requests/$REGISTRY_ID/cancel" | jq { "cancelled": true, "detail": "Cancellation sent to the worker serving the request" } $ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" \ "http://localhost:4000/global/active_requests" | jq '{total, end_users: [.items[].end_user_id]}' { "total": 2, "end_users": ["cancel-2", "cancel-1"] } ``` Three were running, one was cancelled, two remain, and the cancelled one's entry is gone because the middleware's `finally` removed it as the task unwound. For the UI, run `npm run dev` in `ui/litellm-dashboard`, log in as a proxy admin and open http://localhost:3000/active-requests/ while requests are in flight. The page sits under Observability in the sidebar. It shows the KPI row, a filter row, two charts (running requests grouped by model, end user, user, key or pod, and the age distribution) and the table. Sort by Age to find what has been running longest, click any row for the full detail panel with `Open in Logs` and `Cancel request`, type an end user id into the filter and watch it land in the URL so the view can be shared, and flip Auto refresh off when the table keeps moving while you read it. I can attach screenshots and a screen recording if you want them in the thread ## Load behaviour Measured against a live proxy with 12000 entries seeded into the index, which is well past the 5000 scan cap: | | | | --- | --- | | unfiltered `GET /global/active_requests` | 5 ms | | filtered by end user | 35-46 ms, `truncated: true` | | Redis `MGET` at the cap, server side | 4.5 ms per call | | Redis `ZREVRANGE` of 5000 members | 0.9 ms per call | The dashboard held up at that size. A Chrome DevTools trace over 13 poll cycles: every poll 14-34 ms round trip, the 5 s cadence never drifted or overlapped, 50 rows rendered, **zero long tasks**, CLS 0.00, and switching the grouping tab repainted both charts in 57 ms. Filtering to one end user narrowed the page to 121 matches and surfaced the truncation banner, which is the cap doing its job rather than the page silently lying about the total. That is the reason for the cap. Without it the filtered path reads the whole index, and 4.5 ms of blocking on a single-threaded Redis per admin poll is the ceiling this accepts. ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Changes On the diff size: of the 2000 added lines, 812 are tests and 121 are generated API types, leaving 1067 of hand-written source, and 583 of those are the dashboard page. The backend is 484 lines across four files, 327 of them the registry itself. The rest of the backend is a 105-line endpoint plus 44 lines of wiring: the hook mapping entry, the `register_as_litellm_callback` opt-out, the pre-call call site and the removal in the middleware's `finally`. The dashboard talks to the endpoint through the schema-bound client rather than a hand-written wrapper, so `schema.d.ts` is regenerated and the request and response types come from the OpenAPI spec. `networking.tsx` is deliberately untouched. `litellm/proxy/hooks/active_request_registry.py` holds the registry. It writes one JSON item key per request plus a sorted-set index scored by start time, and reads them back with `MGET`. Records carry identity and routing metadata only, never prompts, bodies, headers or source IPs. `user_email` stays out unless `general_settings.active_request_include_user_email` is on, since these records live in Redis and Redis is frequently persisted to disk. Redis comes from `InternalUsageCache` and is resolved lazily on every call, so nothing new has to be configured and the hook does not care whether it is constructed before or after `update_values(redis_cache=...)` runs. Without Redis the endpoint answers `available: false` instead of failing. Registration and removal swallow Redis errors on purpose: this is observability and it must not be able to fail a model request. `GET /global/active_requests` in `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/active_request_endpoints.py` is limited to `PROXY_ADMIN` and `PROXY_ADMIN_VIEW_ONLY` and returns 403 for everyone else, org admins included, because the view is cross-tenant by nature. Both knobs live in `general_settings` rather than the environment: `active_request_ttl_seconds` and `active_request_include_user_email`. They are read at call time, since `general_settings` is populated after the hooks are constructed. Two details worth a second look. Filtering happens in Python, so a filtered query has to read index members before it can match them; `MAX_SCAN_MEMBERS` caps that read and the response sets `truncated` so a large index cannot turn one admin request into an unbounded `MGET` against a single-threaded Redis. And the TTL is the only cleanup path left when a worker dies mid-request, which makes it the maximum age of a stale row as well, so it defaults to 30 minutes rather than something long. `POST /global/active_requests/{registry_id}/cancel` is Proxy Admin only, not viewers, since it changes state. Only the worker serving a request can cancel it, so it keeps the asyncio task handle locally and the endpoint writes a short-lived flag in Redis that the owning worker picks up; a worker that is serving nothing stops polling. Polling rather than pub/sub on purpose: `REDIS_SOCKET_TIMEOUT` defaults to 100ms, which kills a blocking subscription immediately. When the admin call happens to land on the worker that owns the request, it cancels straight away without a round trip. The registry is in `PROXY_HOOKS` for the hook mapping but sets `register_as_litellm_callback = False`, and `_add_proxy_hooks` now honours that flag. Without it the registry would be added to `litellm.callbacks` and run on every logging event for no reason. `MGET` and the pipelines span several keys, so index, item and cancellation keys share the Redis Cluster hash tag `{active_requests}` and stay in one slot; standalone, Sentinel and Cluster all work. ## QA runbook 1. Start Redis and point `litellm_settings.cache_params` at it, then start the proxy with a master key 2. Fire several long streaming completions with different `user` values, as in the proof above 3. `curl` the endpoint and confirm every in-flight request appears once, with the right model, `streaming` flag and `end_user_id` 4. Add `?end_user_id=` and confirm the result narrows to that caller 5. Let the requests finish and confirm `total` returns to 0 and `redis-cli zcard litellm:active_requests:index` is 0 6. Kill the client mid-stream and confirm the row disappears too, since cleanup hangs off the response `finally` rather than a success path 7. Call the endpoint with a non-admin key and confirm 403 8. Stop Redis, call the endpoint again and confirm `available: false` with a reason, and that model requests keep working 9. In the UI, open http://localhost:3000/active-requests/ as a proxy admin, switch the grouping tabs, sort by Age, open a row, and use the filters 10. Cancel a request from the detail panel and confirm the row disappears and the client sees the call end 11. Confirm a proxy admin viewer gets 403 from the cancel endpoint while still being able to read the list ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR `tests/e2e/ui/tests/proxy-admin/activeRequests.spec.ts` covers the page in the browser against the live proxy, no stubbed network: it fires a completion the mock upstream holds open (via an `e2e-hold-s` marker in the prompt, the one addition to `fixtures/mock_llm_server/server.py`), asserts the row appears with its caller, and asserts it disappears once the completion finishes, which is the register and the cleanup path proven end to end. The other cases narrow by end user, regroup the chart, and check the poll keeps running while the page stays interactive. A non-admin does not get the nav entry. The unit tests cover the paths that would silently break the feature rather than the happy path alone: registration is a no-op without Redis or without a call id, Redis failures are swallowed and return `None`, index members whose item key expired are dropped from the index and excluded from `total`, filters match exactly rather than by substring, a page past the end returns empty without losing `total`, the scan cap sets `truncated`, and `user_email` only appears with the flag set. There is a `fakeredis` test alongside the fake-client ones so the pipeline and pagination semantics are exercised against a real Redis implementation. The middleware test asserts that a finished response removes the entry, and the pre-call test asserts that a second registration for the same request reuses the id and start time instead of creating a duplicate row. ## Update: rebased and hardened by six weeks in production The branch is rebased onto current `litellm_internal_staging`; the earlier revision was cut on August 6 and the two new lint gates (`LIT011`, `LIT012`) that landed since then now pass, with every record field qualified `ReadOnly[...]` and the pass-through payloads built as a typed `ActiveRequestCall`. This has been serving a production proxy fleet for six weeks, which is where the third commit comes from. Pass-through requests were absent from the overview entirely: `pass_through_request()` now registers provider routes, and `/vllm/...` and `/azure/...` requests that name a router model take a branch which returns before ever reaching it, so `_register_router_passthrough()` covers those two exits and hands the same `litellm_call_id` to the router call, keeping the overview row and the log entry on one id. The rest is failure paths that only production finds. Redis resolution sits inside the `try` in `register()`, `remove()` and `request_cancellation()`, since a cache that raises while resolving used to escape into the request path. `remove()` drops its local task handle in a `finally`, otherwise a failed cleanup leaves the cancel watcher polling for the life of the pod. The middleware catches `BaseException` around deregistration and decrements the in-flight counter behind its own `finally`, so neither a `CancelledError` nor a failing log handler can strand the counter that gates graceful shutdown. Unfiltered listing now refills a page after dropping expired members and counts the total after that cleanup, so a page cannot show fewer rows than it claims. Filtered listing keeps a bounded one second per-worker cache, which absorbs the five second UI poll. On the page, the age cell owns its own tick instead of the table rebuilding every column each second, and the logs link encodes the request id. Two things in the run logs above predate this: the index key is now `litellm:{active_requests}:index`, and the key field is `key_hash` rather than the `key_hash_prefix` visible in that pasted response. Step 5 of the runbook reads `redis-cli zcard "litellm:{active_requests}:index"` accordingly. ## Review round Greptile scored this 4/5 and raised four findings, all addressed: The key column exposed the first 12 characters of `UserAPIKeyAuth.api_key`. Virtual keys arrive hashed, but custom auth can return the raw credential, so short credentials would have leaked in full to an admin viewer. The column now carries `key_hash`, which is what `UserAPIKeyAuth` has already hashed for virtual keys and JWTs and what the Logs page shows in its own Key Hash column, so a running request can be traced back to its key; anything that is neither a bare SHA-256 digest nor `hashed-jwt-` is hashed before it is published, so a raw credential from custom auth never reaches Redis or the page. The scan cap was a class attribute that a test replaced globally. It is now constructor-injected, so the test builds a registry with its own limit instead of mutating shared process state. `/v1/realtime` and the Responses WebSocket route call the shared pre-call helper with a synthetic `Request` whose state never reaches the WebSocket scope, and the in-flight middleware skips non-HTTP scopes, so those records would have lingered until the TTL. Registration now returns early for anything that is not an HTTP scope. The explanatory comments are gone; the only ones left are the suppressions your own gates require, each with a reason. Latest round ------------ Two things a reviewer of the running deployment caught, plus the two red checks. The Key column carried the salted 12 character fingerprint, which is a value that appears nowhere else in the product, so there was no way to get from a running row to the key that issued it. The record now carries `key_hash` and the table has Key Alias and Key Hash as separate columns, matching Logs; pasting the hash into the Logs page's Key Hash filter finds the same request once it lands. `_key_hash()` publishes `UserAPIKeyAuth.api_key` unchanged when it is already a SHA-256 digest or `hashed-jwt-`, and hashes anything else, so a raw credential returned by custom auth is still never stored. Two tests cover both halves: an already hashed key has to pass through untouched, and a raw credential has to be absent from the record. The Auto refresh switch was wired to pause. It started off, its label flipped between "Paused" and "Auto refresh", and the icon showed the opposite of the current state, so the control read as "enable pausing" while the page was in fact already refreshing. It now reads "Auto refresh" throughout, starts on because that is what the page does by default, and shows a play icon while it runs and a pause icon once it is off. The integration test asserts the initial checked state and the icon that goes with it, and both mutations (starting off, swapping the icons) turn it red. The two failing checks are fixed with those: `register()` returns its id from an `else` block, which puts TRY300 back inside its ceiling, and the integration test uses `findByText` instead of `waitFor` plus `getByText` for the seven cases eslint flagged.

signal.title: [Bug]: PUT /v1/mcp/server silently nulls authorization_url, token_url, oauth2_flow when delegate_auth_to_upstream=true
signal.text: ### What happened? When an MCP server is configured with `auth_type: oauth2`, `oauth2_flow: authorization_code`, and `delegate_auth_to_upstream: true`, any subsequent update via `PUT /v1/mcp/server` silently discards `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `oauth2_flow` — even when those exact fields are explicitly present with non-null values in the request body. The response (and the persisted record, confirmed via a follow-up `GET /v1/mcp/server`) always comes back with these three fields set to `null`. This breaks the Admin UI's own "Authorize & Fetch Token" convenience button (used to fetch a test token for a server's Tools tab), since that feature depends on `authorization_url`/`token_url` being present. It fails with: \`\`\` {"detail":"MCP server authorization url is not configured. OAuth endpoint discovery against the configured server url did not resolve it; the url may be misconfigured. Check the proxy logs for 'MCP OAuth' warnings from server load, verify the server url, or set Authorization URL and Token URL manually, or set Issuer to discover them from the identity provider (RFC 8414)."} \`\`\` Setting `issuer` instead (for RFC 8414 discovery) does not help either — discovery does not appear to run on-demand, and `authorization_url`/`token_url` remain `null` regardless. Importantly, this only affects the UI test button. The actual delegated/passthrough OAuth flow works correctly for real traffic: a client that authenticates against the upstream IdP directly and passes its own bearer token via `x-mcp-<server_name>-authorization`, alongside a valid LiteLLM virtual key in `Authorization`, successfully reaches the upstream MCP server and receives a real tool list. So the runtime behavior of `delegate_auth_to_upstream` is sound — only the persisted config for `authorization_url`/`token_url`/`oauth2_flow` is being wiped on save. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Create/register an MCP server with `auth_type: oauth2`, `oauth2_flow: authorization_code`, `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `delegate_auth_to_upstream: true`. 2. Send a `PUT /v1/mcp/server` with the full server object, explicitly including `authorization_url`, `token_url`, and `oauth2_flow: "authorization_code"` (and `issuer` cleared to `""`): \`\`\`bash curl -X PUT 'https://your-litellm-proxy.example.com/v1/mcp/server' \ -H 'authorization: Bearer <admin-key>' \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ --data-raw '{ "server_id": "<server_id>", "server_name": "example_mcp_server", "url": "https://your-mcp-server.example.com/mcp", "transport": "http", "auth_type": "oauth2", "oauth2_flow": "authorization_code", "issuer": "", "authorization_url": "https://your-idp.example.com/realms/your-realm/protocol/openid-connect/auth", "token_url": "https://your-idp.example.com/realms/your-realm/protocol/openid-connect/token", "delegate_auth_to_upstream": true, "oauth_passthrough": false, "dcr_bridge": false }' \`\`\` 3. Inspect the response, or immediately follow up with `GET /v1/mcp/server` and find the same `server_id`. ### Expected behavior `authorization_url` and `token_url` should be persisted exactly as submitted, and `oauth2_flow` should remain `"authorization_code"`. ### Actual behavior The response (and subsequent GET) shows: \`\`\`json { "issuer": "", "authorization_url": null, "token_url": null, "oauth2_flow": null, "delegate_auth_to_upstream": true } \`\`\` All three fields are nulled despite being explicitly sent as non-null in the request. ### Relevant log output N/A on our end — we don't have access to the proxy's server-side logs in this deployment, only client-observable request/response pairs (above). ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: [Bug]: prometheus_initialize_budget_metrics emits no key budget metrics for keys with team_id = NULL
signal.text: ### What happened? With `litellm_settings.prometheus_initialize_budget_metrics: true`, the background job runs and its user, team and org branches work, but `litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric` is never emitted for any virtual key whose `team_id` is `NULL` — which is every key created without an explicit team. The gauge therefore exists only for keys that have made a request since the last proxy restart. For a deployment whose keys are mostly idle, a metric that is supposed to be pre-populated is empty, and any alert resting on it is silently inert. Nothing logs an error and the job reports no failure. Related but distinct: #29937 reports budget metrics being *emitted with the wrong value*. This is about them not being emitted at all. ### Root cause `PrometheusLogger._initialize_api_key_budget_metrics` fetches keys through `_list_key_helper` with `exclude_team_id=UI_SESSION_TOKEN_TEAM_ID`, to filter out UI dashboard session tokens: ```python # litellm/integrations/prometheus.py key_list_response: Final = await _list_key_helper( ... exclude_team_id=UI_SESSION_TOKEN_TEAM_ID, # "litellm-dashboard" return_full_object=True, ... ) ``` which becomes: ```python # litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/key_management_endpoints.py if exclude_team_id and isinstance(exclude_team_id, str): user_condition["team_id"] = {"not": exclude_team_id} ``` `{"not": ...}` on a nullable column is a SQL inequality, and `NULL <> 'litellm-dashboard'` evaluates to `NULL`, not `TRUE`. Rows with `team_id IS NULL` are excluded along with the dashboard tokens, so `_set_key_list_budget_metrics` receives a list containing none of them. The user, team and org branches of the same job do not pass `exclude_team_id`, which is why they populate correctly and only the key branch is affected. `_initialize_api_key_budget_metrics` is the only caller in the codebase that passes a non-`None` `exclude_team_id`, so the blast radius is this one code path. `GET /key/list` leaves it unset and returns `NULL`-team keys normally, which is why the UI is unaffected and this is easy to miss. ### Steps to Reproduce On a proxy with a database and `prometheus_initialize_budget_metrics: true`: 1. Create a key with a budget and **no** team: ```bash curl -X POST $PROXY/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"key_alias":"no-team","max_budget":5.0}' ``` 2. Wait for more than one `PROMETHEUS_BUDGET_METRICS_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MINUTES` tick (default 5 minutes). Make no request with the key. 3. `GET /metrics` — no `litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric` series for it. 4. Create a team and a key inside it: ```bash curl -X POST $PROXY/team/new -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"team_alias":"t"}' curl -X POST $PROXY/key/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $MASTER_KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"key_alias":"with-team","team_id":"<team_id>","max_budget":7.0}' ``` 5. Wait for the next tick, again making no request with it. 6. `GET /metrics` — the team-scoped key **does** get a series. ### Evidence Proxy restarted at `01:58:59Z`, readings at `02:10Z`, so two ticks of the 5-minute job had passed. Five virtual keys existed, each with `max_budget=5.0` and no team. Same job, other branches, populated correctly: ``` litellm_total_users 1.0 litellm_active_users 1.0 litellm_teams_count 0.0 ``` Key branch, one series, and it is not one of the five: ``` litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric{api_key_alias="",hashed_api_key="litellm_proxy_master_key"} +Inf ``` **Isolating it against traffic.** A throwaway key with `max_budget=5.0` and no team produced no series when minted. One local chat completion with it produced the series immediately: ``` BEFORE 1 series (master key only) mint key, max_budget=5.0 no new series one chat completion HTTP 200 +25s litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric{ api_key_alias="budget-metric-probe", ...} 5.0 ``` **Isolating it against the team filter.** A key created inside a team, with `max_budget=7.0` and **no request ever made with it**, was picked up by the initialiser after one tick, while the `NULL`-team keys still were not: ``` BEFORE 2 series create team, mint key in it, make no request +6 min AFTER 3 series, now including litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric{api_key_alias="null-team-probe-key",...} 7.0 ``` **Against the database.** Running the predicate the filter implies against the live `LiteLLM_VerificationToken` table: ``` total keys | 9 team_id IS NULL | 7 team_id <> 'litellm-dashboard' | 0 NOT (team_id = 'litellm-dashboard') | 0 ``` All seven real keys have `team_id IS NULL`, and the inequality returns none of them. ### Suggested fix The filter needs to keep rows where `team_id IS NULL`. Sketch, **untested**: ```python if exclude_team_id and isinstance(exclude_team_id, str): user_condition["OR"] = [ {"team_id": {"not": exclude_team_id}}, {"team_id": None}, ] ``` `user_condition` is appended into an existing `or_conditions` list, so whether a nested `OR` composes cleanly there is worth checking. Since `_initialize_api_key_budget_metrics` is the only caller passing `exclude_team_id`, an alternative is to filter dashboard tokens out in the Prometheus code after fetching and leave `_list_key_helper` untouched. ### Relevant log output ```shell No error is logged. The job completes and reports success; the series is simply absent. ``` ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.97.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_ --- Environment detail: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, digest `sha256:468c25f35f3e5ec4e414974f00deab93337b1b4d9953cabcfd3722e59415f834`, built 2026-08-16. `litellm-enterprise` 0.1.54. PostgreSQL 16, single proxy process, no Redis, `store_model_in_db: false`. Possibly related and not investigated: a key's `litellm_remaining_api_key_budget_metric` series persists in the process registry after the key is deleted through `/key/delete`, and is still exported on subsequent scrapes until the proxy restarts. Mentioned only in case it shares a cause.

signal.title: [Bug]: False BudgetExceededError under sustained load — 'Current cost' = max_budget + recent spend, no Redis, self-heals in ~2 min
signal.text: ### What happened During sustained batch runs (~100-130 requests over ~40 min, single client, mix of `/v1/ocr` Mistral passthrough, Gemini `generateContent` passthrough and Anthropic passthrough), the proxy starts returning `429 budget_exceeded` near the end of the run, with a reported `Current cost` that matches **no real aggregate**. The reported value is always `max_budget + (small recent spend)`, and the condition **self-heals in about 2 minutes** without any intervention: a retry with 15s/30s/60s backoff fails 3 times, then the 4th attempt succeeds. We reproduced this on **v1.88.1** and again on **v1.96.2** after upgrading, and once earlier when our global cap was 20 instead of 50 — the phantom value tracked the cap each time. ### Occurrences | Date | Proxy version | Configured cap | Error message excerpt | Real spend at that moment | |---|---|---|---|---| | 2026-07-01 | 1.88.1 | 20 (global) | `Budget has been exceeded! Current cost: 20.013879769999956, Max budget: 20` | a few cents that day | | 2026-08-14 AM | 1.88.1 | 50 (key + global) | `Budget has been exceeded! Key=<hash> Current cost: 51.0512, Max budget: 50.0`, then `Current cost: 50.014505` on the two retries | key spend that day ~1.05 USD | | 2026-08-14 PM | 1.96.2 | 50 (key + global) | `Budget has been exceeded! Key=<alias> (sk-...) Current cost: 50.024508499999996, Max budget: 50.0` | key spend that day ~1.1 USD | In each case `Current cost - max_budget` equals the key's genuine recent spend (e.g. `51.0512 - 50 = 1.0512` ≈ the 1.05 USD actually spent by the run so far). It looks like an in-memory spend counter transiently gets seeded/inflated with the `max_budget` value itself. ### What the database said at the same time Checked immediately around the 2026-08-14 AM occurrence: - `LiteLLM_VerificationToken.spend` for the key: **1.07** - `sum(spend)` in `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` for that key, last 30 days: **1.59** - `sum(spend)` in `LiteLLM_SpendLogs`, all keys, all time: **24.90** - No individual SpendLogs row above 0.04 - `/global/spend`: 4.24 / 50 Nothing anywhere near 50, and no row disappeared afterwards. The inflated value existed only in memory and was gone once the periodic DB resync ran (the 4th retry, ~2 min after the first 429, passed; `/key/info` afterwards reported the correct small spend). ### Setup - Docker `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:main-stable`, **single instance**, **no Redis** (in-memory cache only) - Postgres-backed (`database_url` set), default batch-write settings - `litellm_settings`: `max_budget: 50`, `budget_duration: 30d`, `turn_off_message_logging: true`, `drop_params: true`, `telemetry: false` - Virtual key with `max_budget: 50`, `budget_duration: 30d`, model ACL - `router_settings`: `simple-shuffle`, `num_retries: 0`, `allowed_fails: 0`, `cooldown_time: 60`, cross-provider fallbacks configured - Load pattern when it triggers: ~100+ requests spread over ~40 min through one virtual key, several requests in flight concurrently (bounded page-level concurrency). Light traffic (20 sequential probes) never triggers it. ### Expected behavior Budget checks compare against actual spend. A request should not be rejected with `Current cost ≈ max_budget + real spend` while the durable stores all agree spend is ~2% of the cap. ### Possibly related - #27735 (stale spend in BudgetExceededError while `/key/info` disagrees) — same symptom family, but our value is not stale, it is inflated by exactly `max_budget` and self-corrects - #30460 (Redis counters inflating) — we run without Redis, so the in-memory path can inflate on its own ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.96.2 (also reproduced on v1.88.1)

signal.title: [BUG] Virtual key BudgetExceededError uses stale spend while /key/info shows spend below max_budget
signal.text: ## What happened? We saw failed proxy requests for a team-scoped virtual key where LiteLLM rejected the request with `BudgetExceededError`, but the current key/team spend reported by management APIs was still below the configured budget. This looks related to #27639, but this case is for a **virtual key max_budget** check rather than an end-user budget. ## Relevant LiteLLM version `1.84.0` From `/health/readiness`: ```json { "status": "healthy", "db": "connected", "cache": "redis", "litellm_version": "1.84.0", "use_aiohttp_transport": true, "log_level": "WARNING" } ``` Runtime from traceback: Python `3.13` in `/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/...`. ## Setup LiteLLM proxy with: - Postgres DB connected - Redis cache connected - Team-scoped virtual keys - `budget_duration: 30d` - OpenRouter model group Example sanitized virtual key config: ```json { "key_alias": "<service>-Dev", "team_id": "<team-id>", "models": [ "openrouter/qwen/qwen3.5-27b", "openrouter/qwen/qwen3.6-flash" ], "max_budget": 10.0, "budget_duration": "30d", "budget_reset_at": "2026-06-01T00:00:00Z", "blocked": null, "soft_budget_cooldown": false } ``` The team budget was much higher: ```json { "team_alias": "<team>", "spend": 3.546499379999998, "max_budget": 100.0, "budget_duration": "30d" } ``` ## Actual behavior `/spend/logs/v2` showed `15` failures for the virtual key in one day. `13/15` failures were `BudgetExceededError` before the LLM call was made. All failures had: ```json { "status": "failure", "model": "openrouter/qwen/qwen3.5-27b", "spend": 0.0, "total_tokens": 0, "request_duration_ms": 0, "api_base": "", "model_id": "" } ``` The actual error was only visible under `metadata.error_information`: ```json { "metadata": { "error_information": { "error_code": "429", "error_class": "BudgetExceededError", "llm_provider": "", "error_message": "Budget has been exceeded! Current cost: 10.607015384999993, Max budget: 10.0" }, "user_api_key_alias": "<service>-Dev", "user_api_key_team_alias": "<team>", "user_api_key_team_id": "<team-id>" } } ``` A few minutes/hours later, management APIs showed the same key was not over budget: ```json { "key_alias": "<service>-Dev", "spend": 3.536490479999998, "max_budget": 10.0, "budget_duration": "30d", "budget_reset_at": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "blocked": null, "soft_budget_cooldown": false } ``` So the failed request saw `Current cost: 10.48-10.60`, while `/key/info` and `/key/list` later showed spend around `3.536 / 10`. ## Expected behavior The virtual key budget check should be consistent with the spend shown by `/key/info` / `/key/list`, or the API should expose which Redis/reservation counter is being used for the budget decision. If a stale Redis reservation/counter can trigger the check, it should be finalized/decremented reliably so a virtual key is not blocked while its DB/current spend is below budget. ## Additional logging/API issue For these failed logs, `/spend/logs/v2` returns top-level error fields as null: ```json { "error_code": null, "error_message": null, "error_class": null } ``` But the real error exists at: ```text metadata.error_information.error_code metadata.error_information.error_class metadata.error_information.error_message ``` This makes it hard for the UI/API consumers to filter or summarize failures unless they know to inspect nested metadata. Expected: top-level `error_code`, `error_class`, and `error_message` should be populated from `metadata.error_information` for failed proxy requests, or the docs/API response schema should make this nesting explicit. ## Failure summary For the affected key on one day: ```json { "total_failures": 15, "by_error_class": [ {"error_class": "APIError", "count": 2}, {"error_class": "BudgetExceededError", "count": 13} ], "by_model": [ {"model": "openrouter/qwen/qwen3.5-27b", "count": 15} ] } ``` The two `APIError` entries were unrelated OpenRouter parse errors. The recurring issue is the 13 virtual-key `BudgetExceededError` failures. ## Impact Production requests from the dev virtual key were rejected with HTTP 429 despite current key/team spend being below budget, causing intermittent service failures and confusing failure logs.

signal.title: feat(proxy): add per-model strict_token_count to require exact token counts
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Token counts silently understate when a provider cannot count - Clients cannot tell an estimate from an exact count - `disable_token_counter` is all-or-nothing, proxy-wide How it solves it: - Adds `strict_token_count` per model in `model_info` - Marked models error instead of returning an estimate - Reuses the existing strict code path; default unchanged ## User Flow ### Before A developer routing Claude Code through the proxy gets an understated token count for a Bedrock model that cannot be counted, so their context-window logic keeps growing the conversation until the model rejects it. 1. The proxy admin adds a Bedrock deployment whose model Bedrock `CountTokens` does not support 2. The client sends `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "claude-bedrock", "messages": [...]}` 3. The response is `200` with `{"input_tokens": 408}` 4. Nothing in that response says the number is a local estimate, so the client keeps appending to the conversation 5. A later `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages` fails because the real prompt exceeded the context window ### After The same developer gets an explicit error for that model instead of a wrong number, so the failure happens at counting time with a reason attached. 1. The proxy admin adds the same deployment and sets `strict_token_count: true` under its `model_info` 2. The client sends the same `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens` 3. The response is `400` with `{"type": "invalid_request_error", "message": "This model doesn't support counting tokens."}` 4. The client can fall back or pick another model, instead of proceeding on a number that is wrong 5. Every other model on the proxy still returns its estimate exactly as before ## Relevant issues Fixes #37102 ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, format, unit tests) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** (4/5; both findings since addressed) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Shared setup — two deployments backed by the same Bedrock model, one marked strict: ```yaml model_list: - model_name: lenient-model litellm_params: model: bedrock/anthropic.claude-opus-5-20260101-v1:0 - model_name: strict-model litellm_params: model: bedrock/anthropic.claude-opus-5-20260101-v1:0 model_info: strict_token_count: true ``` Both cases send the same body to `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`, with Bedrock `CountTokens` returning its real 400 `"This model doesn't support counting tokens."` ### Before (4fd7a73) #### lenient-model 1. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` `{"model": "lenient-model", "messages": [...]}` 2. `HTTP 200` — `{"input_tokens":408}` #### strict-model 1. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` `{"model": "strict-model", "messages": [...]}` 2. `HTTP 200` — `{"input_tokens":408}` (the flag has no effect; the estimate is returned regardless) ### After (7eb6dc4c74) #### lenient-model 1. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` `{"model": "lenient-model", "messages": [...]}` 2. `HTTP 200` — `{"input_tokens":408}` (unchanged) #### strict-model 1. `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` `{"model": "strict-model", "messages": [...]}` 2. `HTTP 400` — `{"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"This model doesn't support counting tokens."}}` ## Type 🆕 New Feature ## Caveats (if any) - Does not make the count accurate; nothing can without a working API - Converts a silent wrong number into a loud failure - Default is `false`; unmarked models behave exactly as today ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: adaptive_router: one persisted alpha/beta=0 cell bricks the whole router with 500 gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0
signal.text: ### What happened? A model group configured as LiteLLM's native adaptive router returns **HTTP 500 on every request, permanently**, with: ``` gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0 ``` surfacing from `litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks()`. Once it starts it never recovers, including across proxy restarts. Deleting one row from `LiteLLM_AdaptiveRouterState` and restarting fixes it until the condition recurs. The state row responsible: ``` router_name | request_type | model_name | alpha | beta | total_samples sovereign-router | general | gpt-oss-cloud | 1 | 0 | 1 ``` ### Root cause `litellm/router_strategy/adaptive_router/update_queue.py` — the Prisma upsert's `update` branch correctly uses `{"increment": ...}`, but the **`create` branch writes the raw delta as the absolute value**: ```python "alpha": payload["delta_alpha"], "beta": payload["delta_beta"], ``` `adaptive_router.py::_compute_bandit_delta` can legitimately produce `d_alpha = 0.0` or `d_beta = 0.0` (e.g. `d_beta = misalignment + stagnation + disengagement + failure + 0.5*loop`, all zero on a clean satisfied turn). So the **first** flush for a new `(router_name, request_type, model_name)` cell persists a row with the cold-start prior mass dropped entirely — `alpha=1.0, beta=0.0`. On the next proxy start, `adaptive_router.py::load_state_from_db` does: ```python BanditCell(alpha=row.alpha, beta=row.beta) ``` with no validation, **overwriting** the healthy cold-start cell that `initial_cell()` would have produced (`COLD_START_MASS = 10.0`, so alpha ∈ [3, 9.5], beta ∈ [0.5, 7]). `bandit.py:81` then calls `r.betavariate(cell.alpha, cell.beta)`. CPython's `betavariate` delegates to `gammavariate`, which raises `ValueError` when either parameter is ≤ 0. Because `pick_best()` samples **every** eligible model's cell for the classified request type, a single poisoned cell takes down every request of that request type — not just requests that would have routed to that model. Minimal reproduction of the raised error: ```python >>> import random; random.betavariate(1.0, 0.0) ValueError: gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0 ``` ### Notes - `bandit.py` and `update_queue.py` are byte-identical in 1.93.0, 1.93.1, 1.94.1, 1.95.0 and 1.96.0.dev2, so this is not fixed by upgrading. The Auto-Router v2 work in 1.94.0 touches `auto_router/` and `complexity_router/`, not the adaptive bandit. - The failure is silent until it isn't: nothing warns that a persisted cell has non-positive parameters, and the router is bricked for that request type from the next restart onward. ### Suggested fixes (either alone is sufficient; both is better) 1. **`update_queue.py`** — seed the cold-start prior in the `create` branch rather than writing the raw delta, so a new row starts from `initial_cell()` mass plus the delta. 2. **`load_state_from_db` / `BanditCell`** — clamp or reject non-positive `alpha`/`beta` on load (fall back to `initial_cell()` and log), so a bad row can never brick the router. Happy to open a PR for (1) if the maintainers prefer that shape. ### Relevant log output ``` {"message": "litellm.router.py::async_function_with_fallbacks() - Error occurred while trying to do fallbacks - gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0\nTraceback (most recent call last):\n File \"/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/router.py\", line 6387, in async_function_with_retries ...", "level": "ERROR"} {"message": "litellm.proxy.proxy_server._handle_llm_api_exception(): Exception occured - gammavariate: alpha and beta must be > 0.0", "level": "ERROR", "component": "LiteLLM Proxy", "logger": "common_request_processing.py:765"} ``` ### Are you a ML Ops Team? No ### What LiteLLM version are you on? v1.93.0 (Docker `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.93.0`); code inspected through 1.96.0.dev2

signal.title: [Feature]: Make the Usage dashboard’s default time range configurable
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### The Feature ### Check for existing issues - [x] I searched the existing issues and did not find a request for a configurable default time range. Related items: - #12917 changed the hard-coded default from 28 days to 7 days. - #24999 tracks a separate date-boundary issue with the existing “Month to date” option. ### The Feature Allow LiteLLM administrators to configure the default time range shown when users open the Usage dashboard. The Usage dashboard currently defaults to “Last 7 days.” Although the date picker also supports “Today,” “Last 30 days,” “Month to date,” and “Year to date,” users must select their preferred range manually each time they open the page. A deployment-level setting could support values such as: - `today` - `last_7_days` - `last_30_days` - `month_to_date` - `year_to_date` For example: usage_default_time_range: month_to_date The exact configuration location and naming can follow LiteLLM’s existing UI configuration conventions. If the setting is omitted, LiteLLM should continue using last_7_days to preserve the current behavior. **Expected behavior** An administrator can configure the Usage dashboard’s default range without modifying and rebuilding the frontend. The configured range is applied whenever the Usage page is opened. The date picker displays the corresponding selected range. Usage API requests use the calculated start and end dates. Relative calendar ranges such as month_to_date are recalculated when the page loads. Existing deployments retain “Last 7 days” unless explicitly configured otherwise. ### Motivation, pitch Our LiteLLM budgets reset monthly, so “Month to date” is the most useful default for comparing current usage with the available monthly budget. With the existing “Last 7 days” default, users must manually change the range whenever they open the Usage dashboard. This can also make the displayed usage appear inconsistent with the monthly budget period. Making the default configurable would support organizations with daily, weekly, monthly, or annual reporting and budget cycles while preserving LiteLLM’s current default behavior. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? signal.title: [Bug]: reasoning_effort='none' capability gate ignores base_model, returning 400 for Azure custom deployment names (Azure GPT-5)
signal.text: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? **What happened.** After upgrading LiteLLM, every Azure GPT-5 request with `reasoning_effort='none'` fails with: ``` litellm.UnsupportedParamsError: Azure OpenAI does not support reasoning_effort='none' for this model. Supported values are: 'low', 'medium', and 'high'. To drop this parameter, set `litellm.drop_params=True` or for proxy. ``` The `reasoning_effort='none'` gate added in [PR #22953](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/22953) (commit [`6ba2e9f1`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/6ba2e9f10f0d7c309c2f1c1ff56602ee006dbc68), first in v1.82.3) resolves the `supports_none_reasoning_effort` capability against the raw deployment `model` string and **never consults `base_model`**. Our deployments use dated/custom Azure deployment names (the standard Azure pattern) with `base_model` set to the canonical model — e.g. `model: azure/gpt-5.1_2025-11-13_global` with `base_model: azure/gpt-5.1`. The canonical `azure/gpt-5.1` entry *does* carry `supports_none_reasoning_effort: true`, but because the gate evaluates the deployment string (not a registry key, and not `base_model`), the lookup fails closed via the `except -> return False` path in [`_supports_factory`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/utils.py#L2590) and the request is rejected. `base_model` is the documented mechanism for giving a non-standard Azure deployment its canonical metadata, and it **is** honored on the cost-tracking and max-token paths — just not on this capability gate. **Call chain (none of these accept/consult `base_model`):** - [`get_optional_params(model: str, ...)`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/utils.py#L3981) - → [`AzureOpenAIGPT5Config.map_openai_params`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/llms/azure/chat/gpt_5_transformation.py#L107-L132) (`supports_none = self._supports_reasoning_effort_level(model, "none")`) - → [`_supports_reasoning_effort_level`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/llms/openai/chat/gpt_5_transformation.py#L118-L131) - → [`_supports_factory`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/utils.py#L2590) - → [`_get_model_info_helper`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.86.2/litellm/utils.py#L5668) **What I expected.** When `base_model` is set, the `supports_none_reasoning_effort` check (ideally all capability checks) should resolve against `base_model` so a custom deployment name inherits the canonical model's capabilities — consistent with how cost tracking and max-token handling already behave. With `base_model: azure/gpt-5.1`, `reasoning_effort='none'` should be accepted, not rejected. **Empirical confirmation that this is LiteLLM-side, not Azure-side.** With a per-deployment `model_info: { supports_none_reasoning_effort: true }` override applied, `none` reaches Azure and succeeds on every one of our GPT-5 deployments (200, `reasoning_tokens = 0`). Azure accepts `none`; LiteLLM was the only thing rejecting it. **Why this is not a duplicate of https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/25850**: LiteLLM version is different. Also, we suspect that even if the logic correctly matched the custom Azure deployment names to the `model_prices_and_context_window.json` entries, some entries are missing or have incorrect values when it comes to `supports_none_reasoning_effort`. More info on this: ## Additional: registry entries that empirically support `none` but lack the flag Even once the gate honors `base_model`, resolution will still fail for many Azure GPT-5 models because their entries in [`model_prices_and_context_window.json`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/litellm_internal_staging/model_prices_and_context_window.json) do not set `supports_none_reasoning_effort: true` (some are even set to `false`). I empirically tested the following on Azure (api-version `2025-04-01-preview`) by sending `reasoning_effort='none'` and confirming a 200 with `reasoning_tokens = 0` (reasoning actually disabled, not a silent drop). All of these accepted `none`, yet their registry entries do **not** reflect it: | Registry entry | Current `supports_none_reasoning_effort` | Empirically accepts `none`? | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `azure/gpt-5.2` | *(absent)* | ✅ yes | Microsoft **documents** `none` support for gpt-5.2 — clear registry gap | | `azure/gpt-5.4` | *(absent)* | ✅ yes | | | `azure/gpt-5.4-mini` | **`false`** | ✅ yes | Explicitly set to `false`, but accepts `none` in practice | | `azure/gpt-5` | *(absent)* | ✅ yes\* | \*Works on our api-version; MS docs list `minimal` (not `none`) for the original GPT-5 line — please verify before flipping | | `azure/gpt-5-mini` | *(absent)* | ✅ yes\* | \*Same caveat as `azure/gpt-5` | | `azure/gpt-5-nano` | *(absent)* | ✅ yes\* | \*Same caveat as `azure/gpt-5` | Reference for the documented matrix: Microsoft Azure [reasoning models doc](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/reasoning) (footnote lists `gpt-5.2`, `gpt-5.1`, and the `gpt-5.1-codex*` family as supporting `'none'`). Additional consistency issues spotted in the same file (not all tested by me, flagging for review): - `azure/gpt-5.5` = `true` but its dated snapshot `azure/gpt-5.5-2026-04-23` = *(absent)* — inconsistent. - `azure/gpt-5.4-nano` and `azure/gpt-5.5-pro` = `false` — worth confirming against Azure. The base gpt-5 / mini / nano rows are marked with a caveat on purpose: they accept `none` on our endpoint today, but Microsoft documents `minimal` rather than `none` for that generation, so those three may warrant verification before being flagged (the others are straightforward gaps, and `gpt-5.2` is both documented by Microsoft and empirically confirmed). ### Steps to Reproduce **1. Proxy config — custom deployment name with `base_model` set (correct, documented usage):** ```yaml model_list: - model_name: gpt-5.1 litellm_params: api_key: os.environ/AZURE_KEY api_base: https://<resource>.openai.azure.com api_version: 2025-04-01-preview base_model: azure/gpt-5.1 # canonical; HAS supports_none_reasoning_effort: true model: azure/gpt-5.1_2025-11-13_global # custom deployment name; NOT a registry key ``` **2. Send a request with `reasoning_effort='none'`:** ```bash curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' --request POST \ --url http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_KEY" \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"model":"gpt-5.1","reasoning_effort":"none","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"ping"}]}' ``` **Result:** HTTP 400, `UnsupportedParamsError` (see log output). **Expected:** HTTP 200 — `base_model` declares `azure/gpt-5.1`, which supports `none`. **Confirm the fix / that Azure accepts `none`:** add `model_info` to the same deployment and the identical request returns 200: ```yaml model_info: supports_none_reasoning_effort: true ``` ### Relevant log output ```shell litellm.UnsupportedParamsError: Azure OpenAI does not support reasoning_effort='none' for this model. Supported values are: 'low', 'medium', and 'high'. To drop this parameter, set `litellm.drop_params=True` or for proxy. Raised from: litellm/llms/azure/chat/gpt_5_transformation.py (AzureOpenAIGPT5Config.map_openai_params) Gate: if effective_effort == "none" and not supports_none: -> raise UnsupportedParamsError where supports_none = self._supports_reasoning_effort_level(model="azure/gpt-5.1_2025-11-13_global", "none") -> False (base_model="azure/gpt-5.1", which has supports_none_reasoning_effort: true, is never consulted) ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.86.2 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details _No response_

signal.title: fix(responses-bridge): preserve reasoning input items as reasoning_content
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Responses `/v1/responses` requests that replay `type: "reasoning"` input items are mishandled by the chat-completions bridge - Plaintext reasoning leaks into ordinary message content or is silently dropped - DeepSeek V4 and Kimi K2.6 reject or lose context when prior `reasoning_content` is not passed back How it solves it: - Reasoning input items are converted to assistant `reasoning_content` - Standalone reasoning merges into the following assistant turn, or is preserved before a user turn - Opaque encrypted-only items are skipped instead of polluting the prompt - Guardrail text extraction and redaction now cover reasoning content and summary blocks ## User Flow Before: a developer reuses a prior response's reasoning item in a new stateless `/v1/responses` request and the model loses its chain of thought 1. They send `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses` with an `input` array containing a `type: "reasoning"` item followed by a user message 2. LiteLLM forwards the reasoning text as ordinary message content, or drops it 3. The model answers without the prior reasoning, and DeepSeek V4 can return HTTP 400 with `reasoning_content must be passed back` After: the same request preserves the reasoning as `reasoning_content` 1. They send the same `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses` body 2. LiteLLM emits the reasoning on an assistant `reasoning_content` field, merging it with the following assistant turn when one exists 3. The model receives the prior chain-of-thought and answers correctly ## Relevant issues - #36197 — reasoning items (including `encrypted_content`) are silently dropped for non-native Responses providers - Related PR: #27630 (drop-based alternative handling of the same input item) ## Linear ticket <!-- leave blank if no Linear ticket --> ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (lint/format/unit passed locally; CI re-running on the rebased head) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile Confidence Score of at least 4/5 (5/5 on the latest head) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live smoke after the fix (original capture at commit `f6c0cbb49a`; same code rebased onto `litellm_internal_staging` as `ab9c54b6e9` with the guardrail coverage fix): ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "BLSC/DeepSeek-V4-Flash", "input": [ {"type": "reasoning", "id": "rs_1", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": "The secret word is BLUEBERRY."}]}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is the secret word? Answer with one word."} ], "store": true, "max_output_tokens": 256, "stream": false }' ``` Result: HTTP 200, `status: "completed"`, no provider rejection. Guardrail regression coverage: `iter_message_text`, `walk_user_text`, and `build_inspection_messages` now see reasoning `content` and `summary` text; the new tests assert both inspection and in-place redaction. Full local suite: `54 passed` for the targeted guardrail + reasoning bridge tests; `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on the changed files; all three repo gates pass locally. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes - `_transform_responses_api_input_item_to_chat_completion_message` handles `type: "reasoning"` explicitly - `_extract_reasoning_text_from_input_item` extracts plaintext from `content` or `summary` blocks - `_merge_reasoning_only_assistant_messages` merges standalone reasoning into the following assistant turn, preserving chronology when that turn already has `reasoning_content` - `litellm/proxy/guardrails/_content_utils.py` inspects and rewrites reasoning content/summary text so guardrails see every plaintext shape the bridge forwards - New unit tests cover item shapes, merging, preservation, non-reasoning regressions, and guardrail coverage ## QA runbook N/A — this PR adds mocked unit tests, not e2e tests. The live proof above was captured manually. ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(responses-bridge): decrypt proxy-managed previous_response_id for session lookup
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem this solves: - Stateful `/v1/responses` chaining through the chat-completions bridge loses all prior context when Responses ID security is enabled - The client-facing `resp_...` ID is encrypted, while spend logs are keyed by the internal chat-completion request ID - `previous_response_id` therefore resolves to no session and the follow-up starts a fresh conversation How it solves it: - Decrypt the proxy-encrypted response ID before decoding the LiteLLM-managed ID - Use the resulting request ID for the spend-log lookup - Keep the lookup testable without importing the proxy server - Enforce the same ownership check on `/v1/responses/compact` before the shared decoder runs ## User Flow Before: a developer sends a two-turn stateful conversation and the second turn forgets the first 1. They send `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses` with `"input": "My favorite color is blue."` and receive `resp_...` and HTTP 200 2. They send `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses` again with `previous_response_id` set to that ID and `"input": "What is my favorite color?"` 3. The proxy returns HTTP 200, but the model answers as if it has no memory of the first turn After: the same two-turn flow keeps the conversation 1. They send the same first `POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses` 2. They send the same follow-up with `previous_response_id` 3. The model recalls the first turn and answers correctly, e.g. `"Blue"` ## Relevant issues No GitHub issue filed yet. ## Linear ticket <!-- leave blank if no Linear ticket --> ## Pre-Submission checklist - [x] I have added meaningful tests - [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks (lint/format/unit passed locally; CI re-running on the rebased head) - [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem - [x] I have received a Greptile Confidence Score of at least 4/5 (re-review triggered on the final head) ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Live proof against the running proxy (real DeepSeek V4 calls). Before (stock container, no fix): ```json { "status": "incomplete", "output": [ {"type": "reasoning", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": "We need answer user asks favorite color, but we don't know..."}]}, {"type": "message", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": ""}]} ], "usage": {"input_tokens": 95, "output_tokens": 256} } ``` After (original capture at commit `73384cce13`; same behavior rebased onto `litellm_internal_staging` as `c9b0c9e51a` with the compaction ownership and DI fixes, spend-log row flushed before the follow-up): ```json { "status": "completed", "output": [ {"type": "reasoning", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": "We previously said favorite color is blue. So answer just \"Blue\"."}]}, {"type": "message", "content": [{"type": "output_text", "text": "Blue"}]} ], "usage": {"input_tokens": 135, "output_tokens": 45} } ``` Note: the session handler reads the prior turn from the spend-log row, so the follow-up must be sent after the spend-log write has landed. Security coverage: `ResponsesIDSecurity.async_pre_call_hook` now treats `acompact_responses` like `aresponses`, checking ownership of an encrypted `previous_response_id` before the shared decoder runs. Local suites: `67 passed` for the targeted responses/security tests; `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on the changed files; all three repo gates pass locally. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes - `ResponsesAPIRequestUtils.decode_previous_response_id_to_original_previous_response_id` decrypts the proxy-encrypted layer before the LiteLLM-managed decode - `ResponsesSessionHandler.get_all_spend_logs_for_previous_response_id` uses the decoder so spend-log lookups receive the original request ID, with injectable Prisma client/decoder seams for tests - `ResponsesIDSecurity.async_pre_call_hook` now checks ownership on `acompact_responses` requests - Tests cover proxy decryption, the Prisma seam, the no-Prisma path, and compaction ownership ## QA runbook N/A — this PR adds mocked unit tests, not e2e tests. The live proof above was captured manually. ### Final Attestation - [x] The tests check the right things, including edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

signal.title: fix(router): register arbitrary custom pricing thresholds
signal.text: ## TLDR Problem: * Router dropped undeclared `*_above_<N>_tokens` pricing fields. * Threshold discovery depended on input-cost fields, so standalone output and cache thresholds were accepted but silently ignored. Solution: * Preserve declared and regex-matched custom pricing fields during initial and dynamic Router registration. * Select the highest applicable threshold independently for input, output, cache creation, cache creation above 1 hour, and cache read pricing. * Preserve base-rate and service-tier fallback behavior. ## Relevant issues Fixes #34378 ## Linear ticket ## Pre-Submission checklist * [x] I have added meaningful tests * [x] My PR passes all CI/CD checks — all 25 GitHub Actions workflows pass on the current head * [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem * [x] I have received a Greptile **Confidence Score of at least 4/5** before requesting a maintainer review ## Screenshots / Proof of Fix Verified PR head: ```text b64d0a6eee85da7947ab4901f7ba9b0821fd4edd ``` Standalone output threshold: ```text registered_output_tier=1.8e-05 actual_completion_cost=0.018000000000000002 expected_completion_cost=0.018000000000000002 ``` Standalone cache-read threshold: ```text registered_cache_tier=4e-06 actual_cache_read_rate=4e-06 expected_cache_read_rate=4e-06 ``` An inactive input threshold no longer suppresses an independently active output threshold. ## Type 🐛 Bug Fix ## Changes * Preserve arbitrary `*_above_<N>_tokens` fields accepted by `LiteLLM_Params`. * Apply the registration helper during initial and dynamic deployment registration. * Keep deployment pricing isolated from shared backend entries. * Select thresholds independently for all supported cost categories. * Parse nested keys such as `cache_creation_input_token_cost_above_1hr_above_32k_tokens`. * Add output-only, cache-only, and independent-threshold regression coverage. ## Tests ```text Cost calculation: 105 passed Router isolation: 20 passed, 2 deselected Custom pricing: 16 passed Ruff format/lint: passed GitHub Actions workflows: 25 passed ``` All GitHub Actions workflows, including OSV Scan, pass on the current head. ### Final Attestation * [x] Tests cover standalone output/cache configurations and independent thresholds * [x] The fix exercises real Router registration and cost-calculation paths * [x] No dependency or lockfile changes are included
